2.15 · The map: five methods, six posterior shapes¶

Before this: 2.01 (what a posterior is), 2.02 (posterior shapes). You will be able to: name the posterior shapes that make sampling hard; say which method family suits which shape, what each one needs (log-density, gradients, forward runs) and roughly what it costs; read a report card as a summary of particular runs, not a verdict on an algorithm. Optional sections: 6 (concept map).

This notebook runs five methods on six small problems whose exact answer we know, and puts every result in one picture, then in one report card. Keep those two pictures in mind while reading the rest; each later notebook explains one row or one column of them.

import sys, pathlib, time
sys.path.insert(0, str(pathlib.Path.cwd().parent))

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import FancyBboxPatch
from scipy.ndimage import binary_dilation, label, maximum_filter
from IPython.display import Markdown, display

import bayeskit as bk
from bayeskit import problems as P, samplers as SM, diagnostics as D, plotting as BP, style as S

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)

1. The six problems: their size, their forward model and their exact answers¶

Four two-parameter posteriors computed exactly on a fine grid (notebook 2.02 builds them one by one): a plain Gaussian; a trade-off (two slip patches seen from far away); a banana (one station's distance plus a regional prior); two modes (two stations on a line cannot tell north from south).

Plus Neal's funnel in 10 dimensions: a log-variance $v \sim N(0, 3^2)$ and nine parameters $x_i \sim N(0, e^{v})$ whose spread it sets, like a hierarchical smoothing scale and the slip it scales. It appears twice: written directly (centered), and as the same model written as $x_i = e^{v/2} z_i$ with $z_i \sim N(0,1)$ (non-centered). We plot and score it in the $(v, x_1)$ plane.

The problem cards below list, for each problem, the number of unknowns $d$, the number of data $M$, the forward model, the prior and the noise. They are generated from the problem objects themselves, so they cannot drift from what was actually run.

def vec(v):
    return "(" + ", ".join(f"{x:g}" for x in np.atleast_1d(v)) + ")"


def prior_txt(pr):
    sd = np.sqrt(np.diag(pr.P))
    return f"N({vec(pr.m0)}, {sd[0]:g}² I)" if np.allclose(sd, sd[0]) else f"N({vec(pr.m0)}, diag{vec(sd ** 2)})"

How nonlinear is each problem? A single number helps: the degree of nonlinearity NL is the root-mean-square of what the forward model's tangent (its first-order Taylor expansion at the posterior mean) misses, over draws from the exact posterior, measured in units of the data noise σ. NL ≪ 1 means a straight-line model is as good as the data can tell; NL ≫ 1 means strongly nonlinear. The same number over draws from the prior (tangent at the prior mean) says how nonlinear the problem looks before the data shrink the region of interest, which is what a one-shot linearisation faces (a linearisation replaces the forward model by its tangent, a straight-line approximation around one point).

The second number, KL (the Kullback-Leibler divergence), measures how different two distributions are: in plain words, how much information is lost when one is used in place of the other. It is 0 when they are identical and grows as they differ; it is measured in nats (information units based on the natural logarithm). Here it compares the exact posterior with the Gaussian of the same mean and covariance, so it is 0 for a Gaussian posterior. Notebook 2.28 defines KL properly; notebook 2.25 treats both measures and shows how each method degrades as nonlinearity grows.

In [3]:
def count_modes(g):
    """Local maxima of the gridded density above 1 % of the peak, merging maxima a few cells apart."""
    mx = (g.P == maximum_filter(g.P, size=9)) & (g.P > 0.01 * g.P.max())
    return int(label(binary_dilation(mx, iterations=3))[1])


rng_cards = np.random.default_rng(11)                            # separate stream: does not change the runs below
cards = {}
for k, pr in probs.items():
    g = grids[k]
    if k in FUNNELS:
        # exact KL of the (v, x1) marginal from its moment-matched Gaussian: s^2/4 with s = 3. In the non-centered
        # coordinates (v, z) the same model is exactly Gaussian, so KL = 0 there.
        cards[k] = dict(nl_post=np.nan, nl_prior=np.nan, kl=(3.0 ** 2 / 4 if k == FUNNELS[0] else 0.0), modes=count_modes(g))
        continue
    nl_post = D.nonlinearity_taylor(pr, g.sample(4000, rng_cards))["nl"]
    nl_prior = D.nonlinearity_taylor(pr, pr.sample_prior(rng_cards, 4000), m_ref=pr.m0)["nl"]
    cards[k] = dict(nl_post=nl_post, nl_prior=nl_prior, kl=D.gaussianity(g)["kl"], modes=count_modes(g))


def nl_word(x):
    return "linear" if x < 1e-8 else ("effectively linear" if x < 0.1 else ("mildly nonlinear" if x < 1 else "strongly nonlinear"))

Reading the cards: the two linear problems have NL at round-off level and KL near zero, as they must. The banana and the two-mode problem are strongly nonlinear by this measure; the two-mode value over the posterior is large partly because the tangent is taken at the posterior mean, in the empty valley between the islands, where no straight line describes the data. The funnel has no forward model at all: its difficulty is the prior's geometry, and how non-Gaussian it looks depends on the coordinates (the same model is exactly Gaussian in $(v, z)$).

2. The five methods, each with a typical budget¶

Each method is explained in its own notebook; here is just enough to read the results.

  • Metropolis (random walk, 2.16): a chain of samples in which each new point is proposed near the current one and accepted or rejected by comparing posterior values; such a sequence, where each step depends only on the current point, is a Markov chain. Here: 4 chains, round proposals whose size is tuned during warm-up (an initial stretch used only for tuning and then discarded) to about 30 % acceptance (the share of proposals accepted), then 5,000 steps each. Needs only $\log p$, the logarithm of the (unnormalised) posterior density.
  • NUTS (gradient-based Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, 2.18): a chain that moves along smooth trajectories steered by the gradient of $\log p$ (the vector of its slopes in every parameter direction, 2.17). 4 chains, 500 warm-up
    • 1,000 draws each, identity mass matrix (no rescaling of the coordinates; 2.18). Needs $\log p$ and its gradient (from JAX, 2.17).
  • SMC (sequential Monte Carlo with tempering, CATMIP style, 2.20): a population of 2,000 particles (candidate parameter vectors) that starts from the prior while the likelihood is turned up from 0 to 1 in adaptive steps (that gradual turning-up is the tempering); at each step the particles are reweighted, the best are copied, and each takes 10 Metropolis moves. For the funnels, which have no data, it tempers from a broad Gaussian reference to the target instead.
  • EnKI (tempered ensemble Kalman inversion, 2.24): an ensemble of 1,000 members (parameter vectors) moved together by the Kalman update (2.08) while the data weight θ rises from 0 to 1; the update uses only the ensemble's means and covariances, computed in square-root form. Needs only forward-model runs, no gradients and no accept/reject.
  • EKF (iterated), the extended Kalman filter (2.25): replace the forward model by its tangent at the current estimate, apply the ordinary Kalman update (2.08), and repeat from the prior until the estimate stops moving (Bell & Cathey 1993). The tangent is the Jacobian: the matrix of derivatives of every predicted datum with respect to every parameter (here from JAX, 2.17). The iteration is undamped Gauss-Newton (2.10), which, when it converges, stops at a local MAP (the peak of the posterior, 2.08). It returns one Gaussian: that mean and the Gauss-Newton covariance, which differs from the full Laplace covariance (the curvature of the log posterior at its peak, 2.08) when the forward model is curved (2.25). It is shown and scored here as 4,000 draws from that Gaussian. The classic EKF, which linearises once at the prior mean, is also run and printed for comparison.

EnKI and the EKF need data and a forward model, so they do not apply to the funnels. All chains start from random draws of the prior (or of $N(0, I)$ for the funnels), so no method is told where the answer is.

Timing. Every run is timed with a wall clock. Before the clock starts, each method runs once on the same problem with a tiny budget and the same array shapes, so that JAX compilation is not counted. Wall-clock time depends on the implementation (here teaching code: Python loops for NUTS and Metropolis, vectorised arrays for SMC, EnKI and the EKF), while the evaluation counts do not.

In [4]:
class Tempered:
    """Any target written as reference N(0, s^2 I) times 'likelihood' = target / reference, so SMC can temper it."""

    def __init__(self, target, s_ref):
        self.t, self.s = target, np.asarray(s_ref, float)

    def sample_prior(self, rng, n):
        return rng.standard_normal((n, self.s.size)) * self.s

    def logprior_batch(self, X):
        return -0.5 * np.sum((np.atleast_2d(X) / self.s) ** 2, axis=1)

    def loglik_batch(self, X):
        return self.t.logp_batch(X) - self.logprior_batch(X)


def starts(k, prob, n, rng):
    return rng.standard_normal((n, prob.dim)) if k in FUNNELS else prob.sample_prior(rng, n)


def smc_target(k, prob):
    return Tempered(prob, np.full(prob.dim, 3.0)) if k in FUNNELS else prob


def run_rwm(k, prob, rng, chains=4, n=5000, n_warm=1000):
    prob.reset_counts()
    X, step = starts(k, prob, chains, rng), 0.5
    for _ in range(n_warm // 50):                                  # tune the step towards 30 % acceptance
        r = SM.rwm(prob, X, 50, step, rng=rng)
        step *= np.exp(2.0 * (r["accept_rate"] - 0.3))
        X = r["samples"][:, -1]
    r = SM.rwm(prob, X, n, step, rng=rng)
    return dict(samples=r["samples"], evals=prob.n_logp, unit="log p")


def run_nuts(k, prob, rng, chains=4, n=1000, n_warm=500):
    prob.reset_counts()
    out, div = [], 0
    for x0 in starts(k, prob, chains, rng):
        r = SM.nuts(prob, x0, n, n_warmup=n_warm, rng=rng)
        out.append(r["chain"])
        div += int(r["divergent"][n_warm:].sum())
    return dict(samples=np.array(out), evals=prob.n_grad, unit="gradients", divergences=div)


def run_smc(k, prob, rng, n=2000):
    r = SM.smc(smc_target(k, prob), n=n, rng=rng)
    return dict(samples=r["samples"][None], evals=r["n_logp"], unit="log p")


def run_enki(k, prob, rng, J=1000):
    if k in FUNNELS:
        return None
    r = SM.enki(prob, J=J, rng=rng)
    return dict(samples=r["samples"][None], evals=r["n_forward"], unit="forward runs",
                theta=float(r["theta"][-1]), updates=len(r["history"]) - 1, wrms=float(r["wrms"][-1]))


def run_ekf(k, prob, rng, mode="iterated", n_draws=4000):
    if k in FUNNELS:
        return None
    e = SM.ekf(prob, mode=mode)
    draws = rng.multivariate_normal(e["mean"], e["cov"], n_draws)
    return dict(samples=draws[None], evals=e["n_forward"] + e["n_jacobian"], unit="forward + Jacobian",
                ekf_mean=e["mean"], ekf_cov=e["cov"], iters=len(e["history"]))


def warm_up(mname, k, prob):
    """Run the method once with a tiny budget and the same array shapes, so JAX compiles before the clock starts."""
    wr = np.random.default_rng(0)                                  # separate stream: the timed runs are unchanged
    if mname == "Metropolis":
        SM.rwm(prob, starts(k, prob, 4, wr), 3, 0.5, rng=wr)
    elif mname == "NUTS":
        SM.nuts(prob, starts(k, prob, 1, wr)[0], 2, n_warmup=2, rng=wr)
    elif mname == "SMC":
        SM.smc(smc_target(k, prob), n=2000, rng=wr, n_mcmc=1, betas=[1.0])
    elif mname == "EnKI" and k not in FUNNELS:
        SM.enki(prob, J=1000, rng=wr, maxit=1)
    elif mname == "EKF (iterated)" and k not in FUNNELS:
        SM.ekf(prob, mode="classic")


def fmt_evals(n):
    return f"{n / 1e3:.0f}k" if n >= 1000 else f"{n:d}"


def fmt_time(dt):
    return f"{dt * 1e3:.2g} ms" if dt < 0.1 else f"{dt:.2g} s"


methods = {"Metropolis": run_rwm, "NUTS": run_nuts, "SMC": run_smc, "EnKI": run_enki, "EKF (iterated)": run_ekf}
colors = {"Metropolis": S.COLORS["rwm"], "NUTS": S.COLORS["nuts"], "SMC": S.COLORS["smc"], "EnKI": S.COLORS["enki"],
          "EKF (iterated)": S.INK2}
results = {}
for mname, run in methods.items():
    for pname, prob in probs.items():
        warm_up(mname, pname, prob)
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        r = run(pname, prob, rng)
        dt = time.perf_counter() - t0
        if r is not None:
            r["time"] = dt
            r["cost"] = f"{fmt_evals(r['evals'])} {r['unit']} · {fmt_time(dt)}"
        results[mname, pname] = r
# the classic EKF (one linearisation at the prior mean), for comparison only (not plotted)
classic = {p: run_ekf(p, probs[p], rng, mode="classic") for p in probs if p not in FUNNELS}
print("done")

done

3. Scoring every cell against the exact answer¶

Matching the mean and the standard deviation is not enough: an ellipse can have the same mean and spread as a banana and still put its samples where the banana has no probability. So each cell must pass every check below (thresholds are a choice, stated so you can change them):

check pass if catches
mean within 0.2 standard deviations of the exact mean a shifted answer
spread each sd within 0.8 to 1.25 of the exact sd over- or under-confidence
shape 85 to 95 % of samples inside the exact posterior's 90 % region right moments, wrong shape
modes probability of the northern mode within 0.1 of the exact value (two-mode problem) missing or misweighted islands
chains agree rank-normalised split R-hat < 1.01 (methods with 4 chains) chains exploring different places

R-hat compares how much the chains differ from one another with how much each varies on its own; it is near 1 when the chains agree and larger when they sit in different places (2.19 defines the rank-normalised, split version used here).

For the funnels only $v$ is scored (mean, spread, R-hat), because the spread of $x$ is too heavy-tailed to estimate reliably from a few thousand draws even with a perfect sampler. SMC, EnKI and the EKF produce one population each, so R-hat does not apply to them.

In [5]:
def to_picture(k, X):
    """Map samples in the sampler's own coordinates to the plotted plane (v, x1) for the funnels."""
    if k == "Same funnel, non-centered":
        return np.stack([X[..., 0], np.exp(X[..., 0] / 2) * X[..., 1]], -1)
    return X[..., :2]


def score(k, samples):
    X = to_picture(k, samples)
    flat = X.reshape(-1, 2)
    C = X.shape[0]
    out = {}
    if k in FUNNELS:
        v = flat[:, 0]
        out["mean"] = abs(v.mean()) / 3.0
        out["sd"] = np.array([v.std() / 3.0])
        out["rhat"] = D.rhat(X[:, :, 0]) if C > 1 else np.nan
        out["in90"] = np.nan
    else:
        t = truth[k]
        out["mean"] = float(np.max(np.abs(flat.mean(0) - t["mean"]) / t["sd"]))
        out["sd"] = flat.std(0) / t["sd"]
        out["rhat"] = max(D.rhat(X[:, :, i]) for i in range(2)) if C > 1 else np.nan
        out["in90"] = grids[k].inside(flat, 0.9)
    out["north"] = float(np.mean(flat[:, 1] > 0)) if k == "Two modes" else np.nan
    fails = []
    if not np.isnan(out["north"]) and abs(out["north"] - north_true) >= 0.1:
        fails.append(f"north mode {out['north']:.2f} (exact {north_true:.2f})")
    if not np.isnan(out["rhat"]) and out["rhat"] >= 1.01:
        fails.append(f"R-hat {out['rhat']:.2f}")
    if not np.isnan(out["in90"]) and not (0.85 <= out["in90"] <= 0.95):
        fails.append(f"{100 * out['in90']:.0f} % inside exact 90 % region")
    if not np.all((out["sd"] > 0.8) & (out["sd"] < 1.25)):
        fails.append(("v " if k in FUNNELS else "") + "sd × " + "/".join(f"{r:.2f}" for r in out["sd"]))
    if out["mean"] >= 0.2:
        fails.append(("v " if k in FUNNELS else "") + f"mean off by {out['mean']:.2f} sd")
    out["fails"], out["ok"] = fails, not fails
    return out


print(f"{'method':15s} {'problem':27s} {'verdict':8s} {'mean':>6s} {'sd ratio':>14s} {'in90':>6s} {'R-hat':>6s} "
      f"{'north':>6s} {'time (s)':>9s}  evaluations")
for (mname, pname), r in results.items():
    if r is None:
        print(f"{mname:15s} {pname:27s} n/a")
        continue
    r.update(score(pname, r["samples"]))
    print(f"{mname:15s} {pname:27s} {('pass' if r['ok'] else 'FAIL'):8s} {r['mean']:6.2f} "
          f"{np.array2string(r['sd'], precision=2):>14s} {r['in90']:6.2f} {r['rhat']:6.3f} {r['north']:6.2f} "
          f"{r['time']:9.3f}  {r['evals']:,} {r['unit']}")
for pname, r in classic.items():
    r.update(score(pname, r["samples"]))
    print(f"{'EKF (classic)':15s} {pname:27s} {('pass' if r['ok'] else 'FAIL'):8s} {r['mean']:6.2f} "
          f"{np.array2string(r['sd'], precision=2):>14s} {r['in90']:6.2f} {'':>6s} {r['north']:6.2f} {'':>9s}  "
          f"{r['evals']:,} {r['unit']}  (not plotted)")
print("NUTS divergences after warm-up:", {p: results["NUTS", p]["divergences"] for p in probs})
for p in probs:
    r = results["EnKI", p]
    if r is not None:
        print(f"EnKI on {p:10s}: theta reached {r['theta']:.3f} after {r['updates']} updates (limit 20), final WRMS {r['wrms']:.2f}")
for p in probs:
    r = results["EKF (iterated)", p]

How to read the map¶

Each badge is computed by the rules of section 3, and the table above prints the numbers behind it. A badge summarises one run of one implementation on one example with one budget. It says that these checks passed or failed here; it is not a general guarantee, or a general verdict, about the algorithm.

  • Columns are properties of the problem. The Gaussian column is easy for every method. The others are the shapes that break particular methods: a long thin ridge (trade-off), curvature (banana), separated islands (two modes), and a scale that changes across the space (funnel).
  • Metropolis (orange) draws the right picture on the 2-D problems, but at this budget its four chains do not yet agree to R-hat < 1.01 on the trade-off and the banana: in a narrow region the random-walk steps must be short, so it needs many more evaluations (2.16). On the two-mode problem each chain stays on the island where it started (the per-chain fractions printed above), so its share of the northern mode reflects how many chains started there, not the exact weight of that mode. In 10 dimensions its chains have not converged even for the easy, non-centered funnel: dimension alone slows a random walk (2.16).
  • NUTS (blue) uses the gradient to glide along the ridge and around the banana, and passes both. On the two-mode problem every chain settled on the northern island during warm-up and none crossed the empty valley. Its R-hat is fine, because all four chains agree, yet the southern island is missing: R-hat checks agreement, not correctness (2.19). On the centered funnel it spends several times more gradients than on the non-centered one and still fails, because no single step size suits both the neck and the mouth; written non-centered, the same model is easy (2.18). (A NUTS divergence, counted in the badges, is a trajectory whose numerical energy error blew up: a sign of a region the integrator cannot follow at its step size; 2.18.)
  • SMC (aqua) starts from the prior and turns the data up gradually, so particles occupy both islands before the valley between them deepens, and resampling gives the islands the right weights: in these runs it is the only method that passes the two-mode problem. It still fails the centered funnel, because its moves, scaled to the whole cloud, are far too large for the narrow neck (see the 5th percentiles of $v$ printed above). Here tempering handled the separated islands but not the changing scale; the two difficulties call for different remedies (tempering; moves or coordinates adapted to the geometry), which can be combined (2.20).
  • EnKI (violet) matches the exact answer on the two linear-Gaussian problems (up to the sampling error of 1,000 members), with a few thousand forward runs and no gradients. On the banana (one datum), each update moves every member along one common direction, by an amount set by that member's own predicted datum. That bends the cloud partway toward the arc, but members spill out on both sides of it (badge). On two modes it produces one stretched cloud across both islands and the empty valley between them, and θ never reaches 1 before the 20-update limit (printed above; WRMS, also printed, is the weighted root-mean-square misfit, the RMS of the residuals divided by their noise σ, about 1 for a fit at the noise level). A stalled θ is an alarm with several possible causes (strong nonlinearity, too few members, model error, a bug); here the cause is a two-island posterior that an update built from ensemble means and covariances cannot represent (2.24).
  • EKF (grey) is the Kalman update with the local slope (the Jacobian) instead of EnKI's ensemble slope, so it is gradient-based and returns one Gaussian; iterated, its mean here converges to a local MAP and its covariance is the Gauss-Newton one, not the full Laplace covariance (2.25). It is exact on the two linear problems with a handful of forward runs and Jacobians, the cheapest method in the table by far. On the banana its Gaussian is centred at the peak with the curvature of the peak, so it is too narrow across the arc, misses the tips and puts its centre where the posterior mean is not (badge and printed means). On two modes it converges to the northern island and reports it with full confidence: one Gaussian, one island. The classic EKF (one linearisation at the prior mean, printed above) does worse there: its Gaussian sits beside the northern island's centre rather than on it, so only part of its draws fall inside the exact 90 % region, because the tangent at the prior mean describes the data poorly. Iterating moves the tangent point onto the island.
  • Cost and time are printed in each cell: the evaluations in the units each method pays (log-density evaluations, gradient evaluations, forward runs, Jacobians), then the wall-clock time. With reverse-mode autodiff a gradient costs a small constant multiple of one log-density evaluation, whatever the number of parameters (notebook 2.17 measures it). The seconds follow the implementation as much as the method: our NUTS pays Python overhead at every leapfrog step (NumPyro compiles that loop away); SMC evaluates all 2,000 particles in one vectorised call, so its many evaluations take little time; EnKI's time here goes almost entirely into the 1,000 × 1,000 matrix algebra (an eigen-decomposition, 2.06 section 4) of each square-root update, because these toy forward models cost almost nothing. With a real forward model (an ODE solve or a PyLith run per member), the forward runs dominate and the evaluation counts become the better guide to cost.

None of these verdicts is a ranking, and none is a general property of the method: other budgets, tuning or implementations can move a cell either way. Which method is right depends on the shape you expect, on whether your forward model is differentiable, and on how expensive one forward run is.

4. The report card: what each method can and cannot do¶

The same runs, summarised per method. A check means the cell passed every rule of section 3 in this run, a cross means it failed at least one (the first failure is named). Evaluations and wall-clock time are medians over the problems the method ran on. The card summarises these six examples, these implementations and these budgets.

COLS = ["linear-Gaussian\n(Gaussian + trade-off)", "curved ridge\n(banana)", "two peaks with\nthe right weights",
        "funnel as written\n(centered)", "funnel\nnon-centered", "needs\ngradients", "evaluations\n(median)",
        "wall-clock\n(median)"]
NEEDS_GRAD = {"Metropolis": "no", "NUTS": "yes", "SMC": "no", "EnKI": "no", "EKF (iterated)": "yes (Jacobian)"}


def verdict(mname, pnames):
    rs = [results[mname, p] for p in pnames]
    if any(r is None for r in rs):
        return None, "not applicable:\nneeds data and\na forward model"
    bad = [(p, r) for p, r in zip(pnames, rs) if not r["ok"]]
    if not bad:
        detail = f"north share {rs[0]['north']:.2f}" if pnames == ["Two modes"] else ""
        if pnames == ["Banana"]:
            detail = f"{100 * rs[0]['in90']:.0f} % inside exact 90 %"
        return True, detail
    p, r = bad[0]
    detail = r["fails"][0]
    if len(pnames) > 1:
        detail = f"{p.lower()}: {detail}"
    if pnames == ["Two modes"] and not detail.startswith("north"):
        detail = f"north share {r['north']:.2f}; {detail}"
    return False, detail

    ev = np.median([r["evals"] for r in runs])
    tt = np.median([r["time"] for r in runs])
    card[mname] = [verdict(mname, ["Gaussian", "Trade-off"]), verdict(mname, ["Banana"]), verdict(mname, ["Two modes"]),
                   verdict(mname, [FUNNELS[0]]), verdict(mname, [FUNNELS[1]]), (None, NEEDS_GRAD[mname]),
                   (None, f"{fmt_evals(int(ev))} {runs[0]['unit']}"), (None, fmt_time(tt))]
    print(f"{mname:15s} " + " | ".join(("pass" if ok else "FAIL" if ok is False else "-") + (f" ({d.replace(chr(10), ' ')})" if d else "")
                                        for ok, d in card[mname]))

Reading the report card¶

  • In these runs only SMC found both peaks with the right weights. Every other method either stayed on the island it reached first (Metropolis, NUTS, the EKF) or stretched one cloud over both (EnKI).
  • The Kalman methods (EnKI, EKF) matched the exact answer cheaply on the linear-Gaussian problems, and failed the curved and two-peak problems for related reasons: the EKF returns one Gaussian by construction, and EnKI moves its members with an update built only from ensemble means and covariances. EnKI needs no gradients; the EKF needs the Jacobian and was the cheapest of all here.
  • None of the five passed the funnel as written at these budgets. Rewriting it non-centered fixed it for NUTS and SMC; at this budget Metropolis's chains did not yet agree even then.
  • The evaluation counts differ by orders of magnitude, and so do the times. Counted in evaluations, the cheap methods are cheap because they assume more (one Gaussian), and the methods that get the right shape pay for it. In seconds the order changes, because time also reflects how each method is implemented (timing note above).

The rows answer "can it?", not "should I?": an expensive forward model can make even a few thousand runs too many, and a non-differentiable one rules out NUTS and the EKF whatever the shape.

5. Five mental images¶

method the picture needs fails when
Metropolis a walker who tries a random step and keeps it only if it is not too much downhill (a rejected step means staying put and counting the old point again) $\log p$ the region is long, thin, curved or high-dimensional
HMC / NUTS a frictionless puck on the surface $-\log p$, kicked in a random direction; the slope bends its path along valleys; NUTS stops each glide when the path starts to come back (U-turn) $\log p$ and $\nabla\log p$ (differentiable model; JAX) islands separated by deep valleys; scales that change across the space (funnel), unless reparameterised
SMC with tempering a crowd that starts spread over the prior; the data are turned up step by step; each step the crowd is reweighted, the good members are cloned, the bad ones dropped, and everyone takes a few random steps $\log p$ split into prior and likelihood; many evaluations too few particles or too-large steps in β (weights degenerate); moves that cannot reach part of the space
EnKI / EKI / EnKF a crowd that is never cloned or dropped; at each step every member is moved by the same Kalman rule built from the crowd's own spread forward runs only, no gradients strongly non-Gaussian posteriors; ensemble smaller than the number of unknowns (subspace property)
EKF replace the forward model by its tangent line at the current estimate and apply the Kalman formula; iterate to move the tangent point to the peak forward runs and the Jacobian (differentiable model) curvature over the region the posterior covers; several peaks (it reports one, confidently)

box(9.3, 2.45, 3.6, 2.8, "Did it work? [2.19]", "trace plots: hairy caterpillar or not\n"
    "R-hat < 1.01: chains agree\nESS: how many independent draws\n"
    "divergences, tree depth (NUTS)\n"
    "θ and WRMS per iteration (EnKI)\n"
    "a second seed; per-chain energy\ncompare with a known answer")
box(9.3, 0.35, 3.6, 1.7, "Then report", "samples or credible regions,\nnot only a mean (banana) [2.02, 2.32]\n"
    "fit to data: WRMS, χ² per data set\nwhat the prior taught vs the data [2.33]")
for (x, y, t_, b_, c) in methods_boxes:
    arrow(x + 4.6, y + 0.42, 9.3, 3.85)
arrow(11.1, 2.45, 11.1, 2.05)
fig.tight_layout()
bk.savefig(fig, "2-15_concept_map")
plt.show()

saved figures/2-15_concept_map.png

The one-sentence version. The posterior's shape is decided by the prior, the forward model and the data; the method has to be chosen to match that shape (and your forward model's cost and differentiability); and the diagnostics tell you whether it did, without knowing the answer.

In practice. A slip inversion that is linear in precomputed Green's functions gives exact gradients cheaply through automatic differentiation, which suits NUTS; hierarchical scales are then usually written non-centered to avoid the funnel (2.18). A forward model that is a nonlinear ODE or PDE solved by an external code offers forward runs only, which points to ensemble Kalman methods (2.24) or SMC; CATMIP-style SMC (Minson et al. 2013) is a common choice in finite-fault inversion. Network-inversion filters for transient slip, such as the extended filter of Qiu et al. (2018), are EKF-type filters stepping through a time series (2.23, 2.25).
